segments.say: Let's stay with that idea for a while, because it sits underneath almost everything we've talked about tonight. Reactance is what happens when we lose a sense of control. So what happens when we're given a little more of it?

Think about how it feels when someone else holds the remote. You might not even mind what's on. But there's a faint restlessness, a sense that the evening isn't quite yours. Then someone hands it to you, and you end up watching the very same programme, but somehow it feels better.

Is that just a passing feeling? Or can a sense of control actually change how people feel, how they act, maybe even how well they do over time? In the 1970s, two psychologists tested that question in a place where control is often quietly taken away.

In 1976, Ellen Langer and Judith Rodin published a study from a nursing home in Connecticut. On one floor, residents heard a talk from the staff about how much responsibility they had for their own lives. They were invited to choose a plant and to look after it themselves, and to decide which evening they'd like to watch a film.

show.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1976
show.what: The effects of choice and enhanced personal responsibility for the aged: a field experiment in an institutional setting

segments.say: On another floor, residents heard a warm talk too, but this one stressed that the staff would take care of them. They were also given a plant, but the staff would water it. They were told which evening the film would be. Everything was kind. The only real difference was who was in charge of the small decisions.

Within a few weeks, the residents who'd been given responsibility were rated as happier, more alert and more active. They took part in more activities and spent more time talking with others. Watering a plant and choosing a film night are tiny things. But they seemed to carry a much bigger message. Your choices still count here.

Eighteen months later, the researchers returned. In a follow-up published in 1977, they reported that the group given more responsibility still looked better on several measures of well-being. And fewer of them had died in that time, roughly half as many as in the comparison group. Remember, the main difference between the floors had been a small sense of being in charge of a few things.

That last finding is often quoted, and it's worth holding carefully. The groups were small, and a result like that can't tell us exactly what caused it. Still, the overall pattern, that a little more control went along with more life and energy, has stayed with psychology ever since.

show.sub: A small study, a big claim

segments.say: Around the same time, Richard Schulz arranged for students to visit older residents of a retirement home. Some residents could decide when the visits happened and how long they lasted. Others were simply visited. Those who had control over the visits, or at least knew when they were coming, showed clear gains in well-being.

show.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1976
show.what: Effects of control and predictability on the physical and psychological well-being of the institutionalized aged

segments.say: But a later follow-up, published in 1978 with Barbara Hanusa, found something sobering. After the visits ended, the residents who had enjoyed that control declined. Giving control matters. Taking it away again can hurt. It's reactance theory in its most tender form.

And sometimes, control doesn't even have to be used to help. In experiments described in their 1972 book Urban Stress, David Glass and Jerome Singer had people work on tasks while bursts of loud, unpredictable noise played, the kind of noise that makes it hard to think. Some were shown a button they could press to stop the noise, though they were encouraged not to press it unless they really needed to.

show.title: The noise experiments
items: A button that could stop it
A request to press it only if needed

segments.say: Most of them never pressed it. Yet afterwards, they did better on puzzles and showed more patience than people who'd had no button at all. Simply knowing they could stop the noise seemed to soften its effect. Feeling free, it turns out, can matter almost as much as acting on that freedom.
So if a little control is good, is more choice always better? Here the story takes an interesting turn.

show.title: Can there be too much choice?

segments.say: In 2000, Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper published a set of studies on choice. In one, university students were offered the chance to write an optional essay for extra credit. Some were given six topics to choose from. Others were given thirty.

show.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2000
show.what: When choice is demotivating: can one desire too much of a good thing?

segments.say: More students wrote the essay when they had six topics than when they had thirty. And the essays written from the shorter list were judged to be better, too. In another study, people who chose a chocolate from a small selection were more satisfied with their choice than people who picked from a large one.

show.title: Students who wrote the extra essay

segments.say: The researchers called this choice overload, and the idea quickly became famous far beyond psychology. Too many options, and the act of choosing becomes heavy. You worry about picking wrong. You wonder about the ones you didn't pick. Sometimes, you simply walk away.

But science likes to double-check its famous findings. In 2010, Benjamin Scheibehenne, Rainer Greifeneder and Peter Todd combined the results of dozens of choice overload experiments. On average, the effect of having more options was close to zero.

show.what: Can there ever be too many options? A meta-analytic review of choice overload

segments.say: That doesn't mean choice overload never happens. Across the studies, the results varied widely. Sometimes more choice helped, sometimes it hurt, and often it made little difference. The effect seems to show up under particular conditions, for instance when people don't know what they prefer, or when options are hard to compare.

So the lesson isn't more choice, always. It's a real say. A few meaningful options rather than an endless list. Knowing what's coming. And not having that control quietly taken back once it's been given.

show.title: What a sense of control really needs
items: A real say in what matters
Not having it taken away again

segments.say: Sometimes it really is as small as a plant on a windowsill. Something that's yours to look after, on your own schedule, in your own way. Not a grand freedom. Just a small, steady reminder that some part of the day still answers to you.

show.cap: A small thing to care for

segments.say: And this is where it all connects. Reactance and the good feeling of control are two sides of the same need. Take choice away, and people push back. Give a little of it back, and something in them relaxes and even grows.

You can see it in tiny daily moments. Would you like to do the dishes now, or after this episode? It's the same dishes. But one sentence takes the evening away, and the other hands a small piece of it back.

Which brings us to something rather hopeful. If people resist pressure so naturally, and relax when they feel free, then perhaps the best way to influence someone is to remind them, quite honestly, that they are free. It sounds too simple to work. But researchers have tested it.
